title: That is like a Mother!
paragraphs: Love is a ticklish phenomenon which binds the lovers together but prohibits union and attainment of ecstasy. A girl entangled in love is sleeping beside her mother. Her mother’s hand, like a creeper swept by the breeze, is moving around her body, making the girl realize that she is still wide awake.

It is the winter season, specific to the mullai land. The time of the day is midnight. The prayer song sung to appease the presiding deity Kaṇṇaṉ, echoing itself in the hills and trees of the forest, hits the ears of the mother and the daughter, though the actual song ended long before.

All of a sudden, the girl wakes up and sits. The mother without revealing that she is awake turns to the other side. The daughter prays, “Kaṇṇa! Thanks for your mercy! Just as I wished, he has agreed to forget me. On my part, I will not think of him either.”
A satisfied mother goes to sleep with happiness thinking that the mullai deity Kaṇṇaṉ has changed the minds of the lovers.

Realizing that her strategy has succeeded, the girl pretends to sleep for some time, only to nimble-footedly walk her way to the handsome man hiding behind the tree outside. She touches his shoulders and both of them set out on the journey.

The cock which heralds the breaking of day seems to tell tales of elopement of the lover and his condescending lady, without parents’ knowledge, making a startled mother wake up, and realize the disaster. The friend of the girl, who abets the elopement, joins the mother in her grief.

My finely-jewelled girl—nourished by me since infancy, through breast-feeding and intake of jackfruit, banana, mango, and millet mixed with honey—remained under my shadow till attaining puberty, but eloped with an abject novice like cotton popping out of its seed flying away. Friend, shouldn’t we consult the auguries and omens for the wellbeing of the one who left me (though I protected her like a couch shell) and the one who led her away from me? Shouldn’t we seek divine soothsaying? Shouldn’t we take vows to the mullai’s presiding deity Kaṇṇaṉ? Wonder what might happen to them on the way! Wonder what might be their condition right now! Wonder what sort of problems might await them in the future!
Thus, instead of getting furious with the eloped lovers, the kind-hearted mother is murmuring her concern that they should not be haunted by any evil, whomso-ever she has gone with:

> As the heroine goes on elopement with the hero, > The utterances appropriate to her mother are: > She would pour out her anguished concern > To the confidante and to those who had seen the lovers on the way; > She would speak > Referring to predictions unsought and divinations and prognostications, > Weighing the good and the bad that might befall the lovers, > Expressing apprehensions about the path they trod > And about the help that might come their way, > Reflecting on the past, the now and the future of her daughter. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 36).
